text.tspan: Everyday English - C2 - 2026/12/30 - 01 - Essay
A calendar gives plans a place in time.
Pexels · 20657557
Looking back and looking ahead
To make a realistic plan is to negotiate a familiar but frequently obscured relationship between intentional design and the contingencies of shared
experience. The question is not whether arrangements are desirable, but what authority they should acquire. A credible position supports preparation while
withholding the assumption that procedural coherence is equivalent to human value.
There is a substantive case for structure: reviewing a specific experience teaches more than a vague judgement. Here, we describe one habit that helped
us instead of calling the whole year good or bad. The arrangement earns its legitimacy through the specific difficulty it alleviates, not through its conformity
to an abstract ideal of order. Its success is consequently conditional. Once the intervention demands more attention than the obstacle it removes, the
original justification begins to unravel.
An assessment confined to that practical benefit would nevertheless be incomplete, since a small next step is easier to act on than a broad promise. In
concrete terms, we choose a ten-minute practice session and put it on the calendar. This introduces a problem of perspective: whose convenience
supplies the standard against which improvement is measured? An apparently neutral procedure may privilege the preferences of its designer.
Attentiveness to others makes that asymmetry visible and creates grounds for revision.
What emerges is a qualified defence of planning, rather than a celebration of either control or spontaneity. Arrangements can sustain an experience
without exhausting its meaning. Their authority should remain answerable to the people and circumstances they affect; otherwise, a means of making life
more habitable risks becoming the criterion to which life must conform.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a focused main idea. Develop one supporting reason in each body paragraph, with a concrete example. Conclude by
connecting the two reasons without introducing a new argument. Use the structure as a model; write about an experience of your own.
Explain the meaning before looking at the model answer. What two reasons support the main idea? Explain one example. (Model: The two reasons are
that reviewing a specific experience teaches more than a vague judgement and that a small next step is easier to act on than a broad promise. One
example is that we describe one habit that helped us instead of calling the whole year good or bad.)
